10: There are many ways to do bioprinting, but I’d like to highlight one: printing with light. So how did 3D printing start? Back in the 1980s, this man, Chuck Hull, invented stereolithography. He filed the patent in 1984 and came up with the name. We call it SLA. [video] SLA hardens a liquid resin into a solid part, layer by layer, using a UV laser or another light source. (~40 s)
11: Now imagine this for bioprinting. We take a small biopsy, a tissue sample, from the patient. In the lab we grow more cells from it, mix them into a bioink and print the tissue with light. Then it matures in a bioreactor before it goes back to the patient. Because it’s made from the patient’s own cells, the body is much less likely to reject it. (~40 s)
12: The printing itself can be built in two ways. Bottom-up is easy to picture: the light comes from below, through a clear window in the tank. After each layer the platform lifts and the layer peels off the floor. Top-down is the traditional way: the laser is above the vat and cures the top surface, while the platform moves down into the liquid. Bottom-up needs less bioink; top-down avoids peeling, which is gentler for soft gels. (~50 s)
13: Which light do we use? UV cures fast, but it only gets less than a millimetre into tissue, and DNA and proteins absorb it, so it can damage cells. Near-infrared goes much deeper and is gentler, but needs special chemistry, and water heats up. Or we combine both: stereo-thermal lithography. UV starts the reaction, infrared heat speeds it up, and curing happens only where both meet. (~50 s)
14: Two words I keep using. A bioink is the ink of a bioprinter: living cells in a water-rich gel, plus a photoinitiator. Curing is what light does to it: the photoinitiator splits into radicals, these link the polymer chains together, and the liquid becomes a gel that holds the cells in place. (~35 s)
15: So why don’t we print organs yet? First, laws: regulators still don’t know how to classify printed tissue, and it doesn’t fit today’s clinical-trial rules. Second, detail versus size: the finest light printing is very slow, only a few cubic millimetres per hour. Third, misuse: without regulation, a black market in printed organs could appear. And the biggest one: keeping the cells alive. (~40 s)
16: Why is that so hard? Think of a baby in the womb. It is kept warm, at a stable pH, in a protected space, and the placenta delivers oxygen and nutrients and takes waste away. A printed tissue in an incubator gets the warmth, pH and sterility, but it has no placenta: no blood vessels. Oxygen can only seep about 0.1 to 0.2 millimetres into tissue, one or two sheets of paper thick, because the outer cells use it up on the way. So the cells in the middle suffocate. (~45 s)
